3.0.0.en: Bashan: a province bounded on the north by Damascus, on the east by Syria, on the south by the land of Gilead, and on the west by the Jordan River; its land was very fertile and its good things many (Num 21:33-35) (map 15). Edrei: the capital of Bashan, lying south-east of the Sea of Galilee.

3.0.1.en: The children of Israel continued their advance northward to the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, after their victory over Sihon and their taking all his land, as stated in the previous chapter; so the two armies, the army of Israel and the army of Og, met at the city of Edrei.

3.0.2.en: Strangely, Og did not learn from what happened to Sihon king of the Amorites, but came out to fight the children of Israel instead of allowing them to pass; and this was by God's permission, so that they might defeat him and possess his land.

3.1.0.en: Og was one of the giants (v. 11), for the king's bedstead was four and a half meters long and two meters wide, so God reassured them as they went to fight him and his army, for he possessed sixty fenced cities in addition to many villages. Here appears the care of God, who reassures His children before tribulations and hard situations.

3.2.1.en: Indeed God fulfilled His promise, and the children of Israel won a complete victory over Og and all who were with him, so that none of them was left alive.

3.2.2.en: Og rushed to fight the children of Israel relying on his strength and did not take warning from the defeat of Sihon. So be deliberate and examine your affairs so that you do not rush into evil, and learn from the falls of others, and do not be proud whatever your abilities, lest you meet with many troubles and God forsakes you because of your pride and rashness.

3.3.0.en: The region of Argob: a region in Bashan within the kingdom of Og, which included a large number of fortified cities.

3.3.1.en: The children of Israel took all the cities and villages of Og, and Moses tells us their count as 60 cities making up the whole region of Bashan, which is the kingdom of Og.

3.4.0.en: Bars: rods and crossbars for fastening doors securely.

3.4.1.en: Moses makes clear the greatness of the sixty cities of Og, for they had high walls and huge, firmly fastened gates, in addition to a large number of unwalled villages, all this to show the greatness of the divine victory over Og by means of the people of God, who were weak but strong in their God.

3.5.0.en: The children of Israel destroyed all the cities and villages of Bashan, and this was by God's command to wipe out the evil and the worship of idols that had pervaded their hearts (ch. 2:34); but they kept the wealth of the cities, including the livestock, and took it all for themselves as spoil of war, for God permitted them this, whereas at other times He commanded them not to take any spoil, in rejection of everything connected with evil, as happened at Jericho (Josh 6:18-21).

3.6.0.en: Mount Hermon: a mountain extending along the north-eastern boundary of the places which the children of Israel took. It forms the northern end of the Lebanon mountain range, the Jordan River rises from it, and it is said to be the Mount of Transfiguration (map 15). The valley of Arnon: it lies between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers (ch. 2:24) (map 15).

3.6.1.en: A map showing the places taken from Og Lk Asha map (15) Moses mentions here the land which the children of Israel took from the two kings of the Amorites, Sihon and Og, which is the land lying east of the Jordan River from the valley of the Arnon River in the south to Mount Hermon in the north.

3.7.0.en: The Sidonians: the inhabitants of Sidon, a Phoenician coastal city between the mountains of Lebanon and the Mediterranean Sea, 30 km north of Tyre.

3.7.1.en: He mentions other names for Hermon: the people of Sidon call it "Sirion" and the Amorites call it "Shenir."

3.8.0.en: Salchah: a city marking the eastern boundary of Bashan, which was under the rule of Og king of Bashan; the present Salkhad is the same as the ancient one and lies at the southern end of the Druze Mountain, and because it is on the eastern border of the land of the Amorites it was fortified and strong (map 15).

3.8.1.en: The land taken includes all the cities of the plain, in addition to Gilead and all Bashan as far as the city of "Salchah" and the city of Edrei, which belonged to the kingdom of Og in Bashan.

3.9.0.en: Rabbath of the children of Ammon: the capital of the land of the children of Ammon, lying at the source of the Jabbok River, 35 km from the Jordan River; its modern name is Amman, and it is the capital of the Kingdom of Jordan (map 15). The Rephaims: a strong people who were contemporary with our father Abraham, and from whom strong peoples branched off.

3.9.1.en: Here he speaks of King Og as the last of the kings of the Rephaims, and describes his bedstead as about four and a half meters long and two meters wide, and it is in the city of "Rabbath of the children of Ammon." He mentions the great size of his bed to indicate the strength and great size of the body of this defeated king, who, whatever his bodily strength and the strength of his army, cannot overcome the divine power.

3.10.s.en: (2) The distribution of the land and Moses' charge to them

3.10.0.en: Moses speaks here of the distribution of the land to some of the tribes of Israel. To the tribes of Reuben and Gad fell the region from "Aroer," which lies, as we mentioned before, in the valley of Arnon, the southern boundary of what the children of Israel possessed in the middle of the east of the Dead Sea (in whose south the Moabites dwell), to half of Mount Gilead and the cities of the mountain (ch. 2:36). God allowed Moses to enjoy seeing the lands they had possessed east of the Jordan, to gladden his heart, and likewise to look at the Promised Land west of the Jordan River, which they would possess after his death (map 15).

3.11.0.en: Half the tribe of Manasseh possessed the rest of Gilead and all the region of Bashan, which formed the kingdom of Og, including the region of Argob, which is the province of Bashan, which anciently the tribe of the Rephaims inhabited, and which includes sixty fortified cities and lies east of the Sea of Galilee (maps 10, 15). We notice here the fulfillment of Jacob's prophecy to the two sons of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen 48:17-19), that the younger, Ephraim, would be blessed more than the firstborn, Manasseh; for the tribe of Manasseh was divided into two parts, the first half dwelling east of the Jordan and the other half west of the Jordan. As for Ephraim, he dwelt with all his clans in one place, and they were the largest of the tribes in number and had great strength.

3.12.0.en: The Geshurites: the inhabitants of Geshur, a region lying between "Argob" on the east (v. 13) and the Sea of Galilee on the west.

3.12.1.en: The Maachathites: the people of Maachah, a small kingdom on the north-eastern border of Palestine, now called "Beit Jann," lying north of the Sea of Galilee.

3.12.2.en: Bashan-havoth-jair: a region in Bashan that was called the region of Argob until Jair, one of the clans of the tribe of Manasseh, took it and named it Bashan-havoth-jair, which means the villages or encampments of Jair.

3.12.3.en: The land that fell to the tribe of Manasseh was divided between two families in this tribe, the family of Machir and the family of Jair. Jair took all the region of Argob as far as its border with the regions of Geshur and Maachah, and changed the name of the region (that is, the district) and called it "Bashan-havoth-jair"; as for Machir, he took Gilead, which lies south of the river of Jair and east of the Jordan River and south of the Sea of Galilee.

3.13.0.en: Chinnereth: a fortified city on the north-western bank of the Sea of Galilee, now called "Tell el-Azeimeh"; the lake is also called by its name, that is, the Sea of Chinnereth or Chinneroth, and it is the same as the Sea of Galilee or the Sea of Tiberias or the Lake of Gennesaret.

3.13.1.en: The sea of the plain (the Salt Sea): the same as the "Dead Sea," now also called the "Sea of Lot," south-east of Jerusalem.

3.13.2.en: Pisgah: part of the Abarim mountain range lying at the north-eastern end of the Dead Sea, on the southern border of the kingdom of Sihon, and now called "Ras el-Siyaghah."

3.13.3.en: He mentions here the boundaries of the lands which the tribes of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh possessed. Half the tribe of Manasseh dwelt in the north, that is, east of the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan River; then the tribe of Gad dwelt south of it, its lands bounded by the Jordan River on the west and the country of the children of Ammon on the east, and the Jabbok River, a tributary of the Jordan River, passes through the middle of its lands. Then the tribe of Reuben dwelt south of the tribe of Gad, bounded on the west by the Dead Sea, on the south by the Arnon River and the kingdom of Moab, and on the east by the kingdom of the children of Ammon, and the Abarim mountains and Ras Pisgah lie within its borders. The cities which these tribes possessed are mentioned in (Num 32:1-5, 34-42) (map 15).

3.14.0.en: Armed: wearing the implements of war and ready for battle.

3.14.1.en: Before your brethren: you will share with the rest of the tribes in the war and go in front of them.

3.14.2.en: All that are meet for the war: that is, every one of you who has strength to fight.

3.14.3.en: Moses agreed to the request of the two tribes to settle and take their portion in the region east of the Jordan River, but on condition that they not leave the rest of the tribes to fight alone to obtain their portions in the Promised Land, which is west of the Jordan River, that is, the land of Canaan; rather they must go out to war with them until they achieve victory and possess the land, and only then could they return to their own (Num 32).

3.15.0.en: He allowed them to leave their wives and children in the cities they had taken east of the Jordan, and likewise their many cattle, because of which they had asked to dwell in the land east of the Jordan, where there are many good pastures.

3.16.0.en: Beyond the Jordan: this is applied to both the eastern and western banks of the river, and what is meant here is the western bank, where the rest of the tribes would take possession.

3.16.1.en: When victory is achieved for the rest of the tribes and they possess their portions in the Promised Land west of the Jordan, they could return to the regions in which they had previously settled east of the Jordan.

3.16.2.en: This teaches us not to live a selfish life in which we alone enjoy settled ease and quiet, where all our needs are supplied, without regard for the rest of our brethren who are in need spiritually and materially. Rather we must share the cares of those around us, feeling with them and showing our love for them and striving with them as members of one Church and one body, the Body of Christ, and offer our prayers for our brethren and help them, and not rest until we are assured of their passing out of the state of anxiety and need into spiritual and psychological fullness.

3.17.0.en: Since Moses knew that his departure from this world was near, he charged his successor Joshua always to keep in mind what the Lord had done for His people and His standing in their midst to give them victory over the two kings, Sihon and Og. He assures him that the Lord will do the same with them when they meet the other peoples dwelling in the land promised to them, which lies west of the Jordan. And he repeats the same warning to them which he had affirmed many times, that they should not fear meeting and fighting those peoples, because the Lord will give them victory over them.

3.17.1.en: Pay attention to the counsels of your elders and those with more experience than you; rather, may you seek to learn from everyone who is older than you in any field, for it is the distillation of their lives and it is the voice of God directed to you. Your independent character does not mean that you neglect the counsels of others, for this is a kind of pride that deprives you of many blessings.

3.18.s.en: (4) The Lord does not allow Moses to cross over

3.18.0.en: At that time Moses beseeches God, after a short prayer in which he confesses to the Lord His greatness and power, which were clearly manifested in all the works He had done with His people, and that He, God, is the only God in heaven and on earth, and there is no other god who does the same works and has the same power.

3.19.0.en: The stubborn people were, as we learned before, the cause of the Lord's wrath against Moses and Aaron and of His refusal to grant his request; and the Lord's reply was as merciful as it was decisive, for He did not wish to deprive Moses entirely of seeing the land. Moses received many blessings throughout his life and fulfilled his mission faithfully, for which he deserved to enjoy blessed eternal life. The Lord fulfilled his desire in part by allowing him to see the land from afar, without entering it, so He asked him to go up a high mountain, the mountain of Pisgah, which lies at the north-eastern end of the Dead Sea (maps 6, 15), whose summit overlooks the wilderness, and whoever looks from its summit, called "Nebo," sees a large part of the land of Canaan west of the Jordan River; so Moses looked from it and saw the Promised Land (map 6).

3.20.0.en: The Lord asks him to charge his successor Joshua, to strengthen his heart and encourage him, because he is the one who will take over the leadership of the people after Moses and bring them into the land and divide it among their tribes. Here appear the submission of Moses and his obedience to God and his acceptance of His arrangements, for he rejoiced that Joshua would succeed him and declared this before all the people, like John the Baptist, who rejoiced to submit to Christ (Jn 3:29, 30).

3.21.0.en: The valley: the wide valley in which they encamped, in the plains of Moab, adjoining Ras Pisgah. Beth-peor: a city in the kingdom of Sihon opposite Mount Pisgah, the place where the Moabites worshipped their god Peor.

3.21.1.en: They stopped in the wide valley before the city of "Beth-peor"; that is, Moses remained with the people for a time and then went up to Ras Pisgah, and there he died after seeing the Promised Land.

3.21.2.en: May you submit to God's commandments and arrangements in your life, for they are the best thing for you even if they seem contrary to your desires ... He loves you more than you love yourself.

4.0.0.en: Statutes: the duties which God commanded His people, relating to worship and rites.

4.0.1.en: Judgments: God's commandments concerning conduct and the various dealings.

4.0.2.en: Now therefore, O Israel: Moses declares the following words on the basis of the preceding events, which are:

4.0.3.en: 1- God's care for His people in bringing them out of the land of Egypt and tending them in the wilderness of Sinai.

4.0.4.en: 2- God's choosing them as a people of His own, so that they are bound to His commands.

4.0.5.en: 3- Their preparation to enter the Promised Land to live in it in purity, instead of the evil and the wicked whom they will remove.

4.0.6.en: 4- The nearness of Moses' departure from the world, so that he gives them the distillation of his experience, his fatherhood and his guidance.

4.0.7.en: Moses asked his people to listen attentively to God's commandments, which he would now confirm to them, that they might keep them and so be truly His children and deserve to enter the Promised Land; and God's commandments and word give them a life that is not only spiritual with God but also guides them in pure practical conduct in their dealings and all their works.

4.1.0.en: Moses warned them against adding any human ideas to God's commandments, however logical they may seem, because God's word is higher than all human speech. On the other side, no one should rush to remove any commandment he finds hard or unconvincing, for the weakness is in his own understanding and not in God's perfect word; that is, all of God's commandments must be kept. Christ affirmed the same meaning in His Sermon on the Mount (Mt 5:17, 18), and likewise the Book of Revelation affirmed the same meaning (Rev 22:18, 19).

4.2.0.en: Baal-peor: the name of a god of the Moabites, worshipped on Mount Peor, which is one of the peaks of the Abarim mountain range in the kingdom of Moab.

4.2.1.en: Moses reminded them of what happened when they fell into the sin of fornication and the worship of Peor, the pagan god of the Moabites, when Balak enticed them with the Moabite women, so God struck them with the plague and commanded that many of them be killed (Num 25). By this he warns them against turning away from God's commandments and against the worship of idols and evil lusts.

4.3.0.en: You who did cleave unto the Lord: those who hold fast to the Lord's commandments whatever enticements and lusts they face. Moses encourages those who hear him, who held fast to God's commandments and did not fall into fornication and idol worship at the pagan god Peor, and he praises them and reminds them of the grace of life that came as a result of their holding fast to God.

4.4.0.en: Moses warns them of the necessity of holding fast to God's commandments when they enter the Promised Land, for they are their guide in all their life; God had given them some commandments to be carried out in the Promised Land and not in the wilderness of Sinai, such as the Feast of Tabernacles, and what they should do if leprosy afflicted their houses ... etc.

4.5.0.en: Moses draws their attention to the fact that their holding fast to God's commandments will give them wisdom and distinction in all their conduct, which the nations around them in the Promised Land will notice, so that they see the loftiness of their worship and conduct and feel the greatness of their God who gave them these commandments.

4.6.0.en: Moses added that their carrying out the commandments will show God's work in them and His nearness to them and His care for them, and this is completely different from the pagan gods who are far from their peoples and cannot care for them or give them judgments and statutes like God's commandments.

4.6.1.en: Remember that you are the light of the world and the salt of the earth, so hold fast to God's word and apply His commandments, that you may not cause people to stumble by your sins, but draw them by your pure conduct to the love of God who is in you.

4.7.s.en: (2) Remembering the receiving of the Ten Commandments at Horeb

4.7.0.en: Moses warns the people against forgetting what happened to them in the wilderness of Sinai when God gave them the commandments and the Law, because their dwelling among the nations in the land of Canaan and their preoccupation with building and farming might distract them from the most important thing, which is God's commandments. He also charges them to teach these commandments to their children and to tell them what happened at the receiving of the Law on the mountain. This is what the Church is concerned with in the New Testament, namely the handing down of the spiritual life from fathers to children and discipleship within the Church.

4.8.0.en: Moses reminds them of the day on which God commanded him to gather the people before the mountain on which His glory appeared and on which Moses received the commandments and the Law. On that day the greatness of God appeared, and the people feared Him greatly.

4.9.1.en: The midst of heaven: the middle of the sky and its highest part.

4.9.2.en: The people drew near to the mountain, and God's glory appeared in mighty manifestations, namely the fire that blazed on the top of the mountain and the mist, darkness and cloud that surrounded the mountain, to declare God's power and the inability of men to know all that is in Him; for He is the Almighty who in His humility condescends to be in the midst of His people and teach them His commandments that they may live by them and not fear the gods of the pagan nations. The children of Israel who stood before Moses on this day were children and saw this sight. But in the New Testament God's appearing was in a meek and humble form when He became incarnate and declared His commandments in His Sermon on the Mount with simplicity and gentleness. This is the grace of the New Testament, for after we fear God we can enjoy His gentleness and tenderness.

4.10.0.en: The people heard the voice of words when the Lord spoke to them, but saw no form, lest they afterwards make an image of the god and worship the image and forget the true God. The Lord forbade them repeatedly in His commandments to worship images or idols.

4.11.0.en: The covenant here is the Ten Commandments written on two tablets of stone, which it expresses here as the ten words; and the stone tablets represent the document of the covenant that contains its conditions. The covenant is the basis of the relationship between God and His people, and obedience to these judgments represents the people's carrying out of the conditions, in return for God's care for them and their continued sonship to the living God.

4.12.0.en: Moses assures them that the statutes and judgments which he taught them had God as their source, and that it was He who asked him to convey them to them after He had made them known to him. Moses warns them that they must apply these commandments and take them as principles governing their conduct when they take possession of the land to which they are crossing over, and hand them down from generation to generation, stressing the necessity of doing the commandment and not only teaching it. The Lord Christ said in the New Testament, "He who teaches and does," affirming the importance and necessity of doing what one teaches. It is also written in (Jas 2:18), "Shew me your faith without your works, and I will shew you my faith by my works."

4.12.1.en: Do not forget God's former works with you and your promises to Him, so that cares do not distract you from Him or problems disturb you, and let your relationship with God be the foundation of your daily life, so that you live in assurance.

4.13.0.en: Moses warns them against making images of God in order to worship them, for when God appeared to them on the mountain at Horeb to give them the commandments and the Law (Ex 19), He did not appear to them in any form or shape, but they heard only His voice, so it is not right for them to depict Him in an image of their own imagination.

4.14.0.en: Under the earth: because the level of the sea is lower than the land.

4.14.1.en: God gives them examples of the images which the pagan nations make, and warns them against making an image of Him, whether in the form of a man, male or female, or an animal, or a bird, or creeping things, or fish; all of these are creatures which God created to serve them, so how can they depict God by them and worship them, for God is higher than all these images.

4.14.2.en: Of course this is different from making icons of the saints to honor them in the Church, because the saints are created human beings with a definite form, and depicting them makes us remember them so that we ask for their intercession and honor them.

4.15.0.en: The host of heaven: the stars and planets.

4.15.1.en: Divided: God created them for the benefit of all mankind, and every person has a portion and share of them, that is, benefits from them. He also forbids them to depict Him in the form of one of the stars or planets which they see in the sky, for if their love and worship of God weaken they are dazzled by the greatness of these planets, so they depict God in one of their forms and bow down to them.

4.15.2.en: The nations' much gazing at the sun and the stars drew their hearts to them, so they worshipped them; therefore beware of gazing at and being preoccupied with the world, lest your heart be far from the love of God and you become carnal, seeking material things and forgetting God, but always remember that these material things are God's gifts offered to you, and thank Him.

4.16.0.en: The iron furnace: the crucible in which iron is smelted, whose temperature is very high, indeed the highest temperature known at that time ... and it signifies the severity of trials and sufferings.

4.16.1.en: A people of inheritance: a special people who worship God, and He gives them the Promised Land as an inheritance, which is a type of the Kingdom of Heaven; they are holy to God and God dwells among them and blesses them.

4.16.2.en: Moses reminds them of God's love for them, for He delivered them from the harsh bondage of Egypt with all its toils and the mingling with the pagans and their idols that went with it, so that they might live in the wilderness as a special people who worship Him alone, and He gives them the Promised Land, on the threshold of which they have now arrived.

4.17.0.en: Moses warns them of God's justice: just as He punished him personally by forbidding him to enter the Promised Land because of his disobedience to God in striking the rock twice at Kadesh (ch. 1:37), as a result of the people's murmuring and provoking him, so too He will punish severely everyone who disobeys His command by making images to worship them. This is the third time that Moses declares God's prohibition against his entering the Promised Land (ch. 1:37; ch. 3:26, 27), and this shows how bitter his heart was because of his longing to see God's love and the Promised Land, which is a type of the eternal Kingdom.

4.18.0.en: Thus Moses will die on the eastern bank of the Jordan River, and the children of Israel will cross over and possess the land of Canaan. This is God's punishment of Moses, and at the same time he warns them to hold fast to God's commandments and not to worship idols after his death and their entering the Promised Land and dwelling among the pagan peoples who worship images.

4.19.0.en: He repeats his warning to them against making images, lest they be punished by God.

4.20.0.en: Moses shows the power of God's justice, likening Him to a consuming fire, that is, one that destroys everyone who persists in disobeying Him.

4.20.1.en: He also points to God's intense love for His people, likening it to the love of a bridegroom for his bride, for whom he is jealous over her inclination to any other man besides him, so that he takes vengeance on her and on him; so too God is a jealous God who punishes His people severely if they leave Him and worship another god besides Him, especially after all the love and care they have received from Him, for their rest and good are in worshipping Him and living with Him.

4.21.0.en: Moses also warns them that after their settling in the land of Canaan for many years and the birth of children and grandchildren, they may forget God's commandments and imitate the pagan nations around them, making images like them and worshipping them, because a person's material settledness very often invites him to laxity, so that he neglects the worship of God.

4.22.0.en: Heaven and earth: what is meant is the inanimate creatures obedient to God, and also those in them, the angels in heaven and men on earth.

4.22.1.en: God testifies against them that if they disobey His commandments and worship idols, they will perish and be driven from this land, because it is God's gift to them; if they do not obey Him, He will take it from them and remove them from it.

4.23.0.en: God threatens them that they will be scattered among the nations of the earth and their numbers will dwindle, so that they become a small people of no value among the peoples of the earth, and this is what happened during the captivity.

4.24.0.en: In the places to which God will drive them they will live among the pagans, so they will sink down like them and make lifeless images and, sadly, worship them.

4.24.1.en: It appears here that Moses' warnings to them include details which he knew by the spirit of prophecy, so he warns his people in the hope that they will take heed and hold fast to God's commandments and His worship.

4.25.s.en: (4) There is none other besides God

4.25.0.en: God's tenderness toward His people appears in that, although they fell into the worship of idols and were punished with captivity and driven from their land to scattered places in the world, yet if they repent there and seek God, He forgives them and they find help from Him that supports them and rescues them from captivity. But the condition is that the repentance be with all the heart and the seeking of God with complete faith, that is, refusing to rely on pagan gods and all the powers of the world.

4.26.0.en: When thou art in tribulation: God punished you with captivity and driving out from your land to other, foreign countries.

4.26.1.en: The latter days: after the completion of the punishment by captivity.

4.26.2.en: God allows His people to be disciplined for a full period, which is the period of the captivity, and at its end the people feel their error and repent, and God receives them, and their inner senses are opened and they care to hear God's commandments and worship Him faithfully, so He has mercy on them and removes from them all discipline. It also means that in the latter days, that is, in the fullness of time, God's mercy appears in the incarnation of Christ to redeem His people and everyone who believes in Him.

4.27.0.en: He affirms here God's mercy, which appears in His holding fast to His covenant with His people, which He gave to the fathers "Abraham, Isaac and Jacob" by blessing their descendants, so He forgives them their sins and brings them back from captivity to their country, as happened at the hands of Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah (Ezra 1, 2; Neh 7, 8) and as happened by the incarnation of Christ.

4.28.0.en: The days that are past: from the creation of the world.

4.28.1.en: From the one side of heaven unto the other: that is, every place on earth, from east to west and from north to south.

4.28.2.en: Moses shows God's care for His people, which has not happened with any other people in the world, and God draws His people's attention to ponder it, for it has not happened with any people since the creation of the world and in every place on earth.

4.29.0.en: He reminds them of God's grace that appeared in His speaking with them from the mountain, when He gave Moses the commandments and the Law and appeared in the form of a great fire on the mountain, yet it did not burn the people and they did not die because of the greatness of God's voice, but enjoyed, unlike the other peoples of the earth, hearing His voice and rejoicing in His care.

4.30.0.en: He declares another manifestation of God's care, which is His choosing them as a special people for Himself and bringing them out from the midst of a great nation, the people of Egypt, which was reckoned the strongest of peoples at that time, and this by a great divine power which appeared in the ten plagues and then the crossing of the Red Sea and the destruction of the Egyptians.

4.31.0.en: The people of God saw with their own eyes all that God did with them in Egypt and in the wilderness of Sinai, and these wonders declare that He is the only God and that all the gods of the pagan nations are demons.

4.32.0.en: The purpose of hearing God's voice is to plant His fear in the heart of His people, which was also manifested in seeing Him in His great fire on the mountain in Sinai; for God's voice and seeing Him in the fire declare that He is the only God, who loves His people and shepherds them.

4.33.0.en: In His sight: Himself, by means of His dwelling in the midst of His people.

4.33.1.en: God's love appeared in His holding fast to His promises to the fathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, so He delivered their descendants, that is, His people, from the bondage of Egypt by means of the ten plagues, and led them by the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire, which declares His dwelling in their midst, and took them through the Red Sea and drowned Pharaoh and all his army.

4.34.0.en: After their departure from Egypt God also led them to victory over peoples stronger than they, so He drove out kings before them, such as Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan (ch. 2, 3), and gave the land of these kings to two and a half of their tribes. Indeed He will also drive out the Canaanites from the western bank of the Jordan River and give their land to the rest of the tribes of Israel.

4.35.0.en: The final result of all the foregoing is the confidence of God's people in Him that He is the only God in heaven and on earth, and that everything the pagans claim as gods in heaven or on earth are demons, and the people of God must repeat this faith in order to establish it in their hearts.

4.35.1.en: Repeating the Psalms and verses reminds us of God's presence with us, so it gives reassurance to our hearts and also gives us His fear, so we guard against sin and keep far from it, and if we sin we repent quickly.

4.36.0.en: As a result of faith in the one God and in His great power, love and care for His people, His children must hold fast to His commandments and laws throughout their lives, and God will keep them and their children in peace and give them a long life and an enjoyment of their days with God that extends into eternity by their being with Him in the Kingdom of Heaven.

4.37.0.en: On this side Jordan toward the sunrising: on the eastern bank of the Jordan River.

4.37.1.en: Bezer: it lies about 30 km north-east of the Dead Sea.

4.37.2.en: Ramoth in Gilead: it lies about 45 km east of the Sea of Galilee.

4.37.3.en: Golan: north-east of the Sea of Galilee (map 11).

4.37.4.en: Moses designated three cities on the eastern bank of the Jordan, where the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh settled: one in the south where the tribe of Reuben is, which is Bezer; the second in the middle where the tribe of Gad is, which is Ramoth in Gilead; and the third in the north within the borders of half the tribe of Manasseh, which is Golan.

4.37.5.en: God appointed these cities so that anyone who killed a person unintentionally might flee to them. Since the custom of taking vengeance was common in Bedouin societies, including Israel, it was necessary to set aside these cities for this purpose.

4.37.6.en: As we shall see later, three other cities were designated on the western bank to serve the same purpose for the tribes that would settle there.

4.37.7.en: With this the first sermon of Moses the prophet ends, which began at the beginning of this book, and the second sermon begins at the next verse.

4.37.8.en: If a person is hard in his feelings because of his selfishness, so that he takes vengeance on the one who killed one of his loved ones, yet God's mercy preserves even sinners, especially those who sin unintentionally as long as they repent, just as He appointed the cities of refuge for one who falls into accidental killing. Therefore trust in God's mercies whatever your sins, for He loves you and wants your salvation.

4.38.0.en: The law: the Law, which includes the divine commands and ordinances that Moses received from God on the mountain.

4.38.1.en: The testimonies: God's commandments and judgments, which bear witness to the existence of God and bear witness against the people so that they hold fast to them and do not transgress them.

4.38.2.en: This is the introduction to the second sermon of Moses, in which he repeats the divine commandments and laws that he had mentioned before in (Ex 20-23); he repeats them here because the fathers who heard them in the Book of Exodus have died, and these are their sons who will enter the Promised Land. Therefore this book was called Deuteronomy, that is, the repetition and confirmation of the Law, and the sermon will extend from here to (ch. 26:19).

4.39.0.en: Beyond the Jordan: the eastern bank of the Jordan.

4.39.1.en: Peor: the temple of the god Peor, the god of the Moabites.

4.39.3.en: The land of Sihon: it lies east of the Jordan (Num 21:25-27; ch. 2:24).

4.39.4.en: Heshbon: the capital of the Amorites, whose king was Sihon.

4.39.5.en: The land of Og: it lies east of the Jordan River (ch. 3:1). Aroer: a Moabite city (ch. 2:36). The valley of Arnon): ch. 2:24.(The Arabah: the region between the Dead Sea and the Red Sea.

4.39.6.en: Mount Sion: the same as Mount Hermon (ch. 3:8). The sea of the plain: the Dead Sea (map 15). Moses makes clear the place where he delivered this second sermon of his (map 15), and also makes clear the people's possession of the land which Sihon had held, and also the land which Og king of Bashan had held, both lands being on the eastern bank of the Jordan. Then he defined geographically the boundaries of those lands from the city of Aroer, which is on the edge of the valley of Arnon, in the south, to Mount Hermon in the north, that is, the whole region through which the Jordan River, the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea run, below the slopes of Mount Pisgah, on the eastern side of the river.

4.39.7.en: God repeats His voice to us more than once and in more than one way so that we do not forget His commandments, out of His concern for our salvation. May we give heed to His voice and hasten to carry out His commandments.
